claim: The medial geniculate body (MGB) is the auditory thalamus.
source: We studied learning-related activity in the medial geniculate body (MGB; Auditory thalamus), targeting mainly the dorsal and medial regions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a definitional statement.

claim: The MGB was tuned to frequency.
source: The MGB was tuned to frequency and responded to cognitive features like the choice of the mouse within several hundred milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations reported in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1F-I.

claim: The MGB responded to cognitive features like the choice of the mouse within several hundred milliseconds.
source: The MGB was tuned to frequency and responded to cognitive features like the choice of the mouse within several hundred milliseconds.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing temporal dynamics of choice encoding.

claim: Encoding of choice in the MGB increased with learning.
source: Encoding of choice in the MGB increased with learning, and was highly correlated with the learning curves of the mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements across learning phases.

claim: Encoding of choice in the MGB was highly correlated with the learning curves of the mice.
source: Encoding of choice in the MGB increased with learning, and was highly correlated with the learning curves of the mice.
evidence: This correlation is quantified in the results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: MGB encoded motor parameters of the mouse during the task.
source: MGB also encoded motor parameters of the mouse during the task.
evidence: This is supported by body movement tracking data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The MGB encodes task-related information.
source: These results provide evidence that the MGB encodes task- motor- and learning-related information.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: The MGB encodes learning-related information.
source: These results provide evidence that the MGB encodes task- motor- and learning-related information.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between MGB responses and learning curves.

claim: Learning to discriminate between different sensory stimuli leads to changes in primary sensory areas.
source: For example, learning to discriminate between different sensory stimuli leads to changes in the respective primary sensory areas (Blake et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2015; Driscoll et al., 2017; Gilad and Helmchen, 2020; Jurjut et al., 2017; Komiyama et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Poort et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical neural responses strengthen after learning in animals that gain expertise in a specific task.
source: For example, neural signals in animals that gain expertise in a specific task, show increased activity and result in higher discriminatory power between the learned stimuli (Gilad et al., 2018; Gilad and Helmchen, 2020; Poort et al., 2015; Wiest et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreased responsiveness to learned stimuli may result in improvement in the discrimination of the stimuli.
source: In other cases, decreased responsiveness to the learned stimuli have been measured. These changes, too, may result in improvement in the discrimination of the stimuli (Christensen et al., 2019; Maor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thalamocortical circuitry encodes high-order processing of cognitive functions such as attention, working memory and learning.
source: Rather, thalamocortical circuitry also encodes high-order processing of cognitive functions such as attention, working memory and learning (Acsády, 2017; Audette et al., 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Bolkan et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; McAlonan et al., 2008; Rose and Bonhoeffer, 2018; Roth et al., 2016; Saalmann and Kastner, 2015; Schmitt et al., 2017; Ward, 2013; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Zhang and Bruno, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The MGB predominantly receives direct input from the inferior colliculus.
source: The MGB is, at least in part, a thalamic relay center of the auditory pathway, predominantly receiving direct input from the inferior colliculus (Calford and Aitkin, 1983; Peruzzi et al., 1997), but also from cortex (Winer et al., 2001) and other sources (Crabtree, 1998; Lee, 2015; Winer, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The MGB receives input from cortex.
source: The MGB is, at least in part, a thalamic relay center of the auditory pathway, predominantly receiving direct input from the inferior colliculus (Calford and Aitkin, 1983; Peruzzi et al., 1997), but also from cortex (Winer et al., 2001) and other sources (Crabtree, 1998; Lee, 2015; Winer, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: MGB projections target the cerebral cortex.
source: Its projections target the cerebral cortex and numerous other brain areas such as the amygdala (LeDoux et al., 1991; Lee, 2015; Tasaka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: MGB projections target the amygdala.
source: Its projections target the cerebral cortex and numerous other brain areas such as the amygdala (LeDoux et al., 1991; Lee, 2015; Tasaka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Anatomical studies divide the MGB into three main sub-divisions: ventral, dorsal and medial.
source: Anatomical studies divide the MGB into three main sub-divisions: ventral, dorsal and medial (Calford and Aitkin, 1983; Clerici and Coleman, 1990; Hashikawa et al., 1991; Imig and Morel, 1985; Mo and Sherman, 2019; Rouiller et al., 1989; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The ventral MGB relays topographically organized information from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex.
source: The ventral MGB relays topographically organized information from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex (Rouiller et al., 1989; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The lemniscal pathway is considered to be the main auditory processing pathway.
source: This pathway is called the lemniscal pathway, and is considered to be the main auditory processing pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: The dorsal and medial parts of the MGB process more complex information than the ventral MGB and do not obey strict tonotopy.
source: Particularly, the dorsal and medial parts of the MGB are thought to process more complex information than the ventral MGB and not obey strict tonotopy.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical and functional knowledge.

claim: Dorsal and medial MGB project to higher-order cortical areas.
source: Dorsal and medial MGB project to higher-order cortical areas (Huang and Winer, 2000; Lee, 2015; Tasaka et al., 2020) and receive cortical feedback, among others, from layer 5 of the auditory cortex (Bartlett et al., 2000; Lee, 2015; Llano and Sherman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Dorsal and medial MGB receive cortical feedback from layer 5 of the auditory cortex.
source: Dorsal and medial MGB project to higher-order cortical areas (Huang and Winer, 2000; Lee, 2015; Tasaka et al., 2020) and receive cortical feedback, among others, from layer 5 of the auditory cortex (Bartlett et al., 2000; Lee, 2015; Llano and Sherman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: After training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display encoding of higher-order choice information.
source: Learning-related plasticity has been measured in the cortex after training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display several learning related modulations: encoding of higher-order choice information (Guo et al., 2019; Jaramillo et al., 2014), tonotopic map reorganization (Maor et al., 2020; Polley et al., 2006), increased responses to a target frequency and decreased responses to a distractor stimulus (Blake et al., 2002; David et al., 2012; Ghose, 2004; Ohl and Scheich, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: After training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display tonotopic map reorganization.
source: Learning-related plasticity has been measured in the cortex after training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display several learning related modulations: encoding of higher-order choice information (Guo et al., 2019; Jaramillo et al., 2014), tonotopic map reorganization (Maor et al., 2020; Polley et al., 2006), increased responses to a target frequency and decreased responses to a distractor stimulus (Blake et al., 2002; David et al., 2012; Ghose, 2004; Ohl and Scheich, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: After training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display increased responses to a target frequency and decreased responses to a distractor stimulus.
source: Learning-related plasticity has been measured in the cortex after training animals to discriminate between two simple sounds, neurons in auditory cortex display several learning related modulations: encoding of higher-order choice information (Guo et al., 2019; Jaramillo et al., 2014), tonotopic map reorganization (Maor et al., 2020; Polley et al., 2006), increased responses to a target frequency and decreased responses to a distractor stimulus (Blake et al., 2002; David et al., 2012; Ghose, 2004; Ohl and Scheich, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The inferior colliculus processes auditory information based on behavioral context and bodily movements.
source: The inferior colliculus, too, has been shown to processes auditory information based on behavioral context and bodily movements, which are also considered high order processing (Calford and Aitkin, 1983; Casseday et al., 2002; Gruters and Groh, 2012; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The MGB has been shown to encode the choice of the mouse during an auditory discrimination task.
source: Indeed, the MGB has been shown to encode the choice of the mouse during an auditory discrimination task (Chen et al., 2019; Jaramillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A large body of evidence indicates that the medial MGB is involved in auditory fear conditioning by providing fast, less refined auditory information to the lateral amygdala.
source: Furthermore, a large body of evidence indicates that the medial MGB is involved in auditory fear conditioning, by providing fast, less refined auditory information to the lateral amygdala (Han et al., 2008; Herry and Johansen, 2014; Maren and Quirk, 2004; Quirk et al., 1995; Romanski and LeDoux, 1992; Weinberger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AAV-GCaMP6f was injected into the MGB of C57BL/6 mice.
source: To study learning-related changes in the MGB, we injected AAV-GCaMP6f into the MGB of C57BL/6 mice and implanted a 400 µm optical fiber directly above the injection site.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: A 400 µm optical fiber was implanted directly above the MGB injection site.
source: To study learning-related changes in the MGB, we injected AAV-GCaMP6f into the MGB of C57BL/6 mice and implanted a 400 µm optical fiber directly above the injection site.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Mice were trained on a go/no-go auditory discrimination task after a week of handling and habituation to head-fixation.
source: After a week of handling and habituation to head-fixation, we trained mice on a go/no-go auditory discrimination task.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Each trial started with a visual start cue (orange LED; duration 0.1 s; 2 s before stimulus onset).
source: Each trial started with a visual start cue (orange LED; duration 0.1 s; 2 s before stimulus onset) followed by an auditory stimulus, either a go or a no-go pure tone sound (Figure 1A; duration 1 s; sounds separated by 0.5 octave; mostly 10 kHz for go and 7.1 kHz for no-go; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The auditory stimulus was either a go or a no-go pure tone sound with duration 1 s and sounds separated by 0.5 octave.
source: Each trial started with a visual start cue (orange LED; duration 0.1 s; 2 s before stimulus onset) followed by an auditory stimulus, either a go or a no-go pure tone sound (Figure 1A; duration 1 s; sounds separated by 0.5 octave; mostly 10 kHz for go and 7.1 kHz for no-go; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The go sound was mostly 10 kHz and the no-go sound was mostly 7.1 kHz.
source: Each trial started with a visual start cue (orange LED; duration 0.1 s; 2 s before stimulus onset) followed by an auditory stimulus, either a go or a no-go pure tone sound (Figure 1A; duration 1 s; sounds separated by 0.5 octave; mostly 10 kHz for go and 7.1 kHz for no-go; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Licking in response to the go sound were counted as 'hit' trials and rewarded with a drop of water.
source: Licking in response to the go sound were counted as 'hit' trials and rewarded with a drop of water.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Withholding licking in response to the no-go sound were counted as correct rejection trials (CR), and were not punished or reinforced.
source: Withholding licking in response to the no-go sound were counted as correct rejection trials (CR), and were not punished or reinforced.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Licking in response to the no-go sound were counted as false alarm trials (FA) that were followed by a mild punishment in the form of white noise (duration 3 s).
source: Licking in response to the no-go sound were counted as false alarm trials (FA) that were followed by a mild punishment in the form of white noise (duration 3 s).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Withholding licking for the go sound were counted as Miss trials, and were not punished.
source: Withholding licking for the go sound were counted as Miss trials, and were not punished.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The fiber tips of the six mice were reconstructed to the higher-order regions of the MGB (medial and dorsal parts).
source: The fiber tips of the six mice were reconstructed to the higher-order regions of the MGB (Figure 1C, medial and dorsal parts grouped as MGB for simplicity).
evidence: This is demonstrated through histological reconstruction shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice learned the task within 1200–2000 trials as assessed by d'.
source: Mice learned the task within 1200–2000 trials as assessed by d' (defined as d'=Z(Hit/(Hit+Miss)) – Z(FA/(FA+CR) where Z denotes the inverse of the cumulative distribution function; performance threshold was defined as d'=1; Figure 1D,E; fitted with a sigmoid function (Bathellier et al., 2013; Maor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Performance threshold was defined as d'=1.
source: Mice learned the task within 1200–2000 trials as assessed by d' (defined as d'=Z(Hit/(Hit+Miss)) – Z(FA/(FA+CR) where Z denotes the inverse of the cumulative distribution function; performance threshold was defined as d'=1; Figure 1D,E; fitted with a sigmoid function (Bathellier et al., 2013; Maor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: Individual mice varied widely in performance and strategy during learning.
source: The learning curves with respect to the go and no-go trials shows that individual mice varied widely in performance and strategy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some mice increased their CR rate during learning.
source: Learning the task took different forms: some mice increased their CR rate, others had a steep increase in hit rate, whereas others gradually increased both hit and CR rates.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Some mice had a steep increase in hit rate during learning.
source: Learning the task took different forms: some mice increased their CR rate, others had a steep increase in hit rate, whereas others gradually increased both hit and CR rates.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Some mice gradually increased both hit and CR rates during learning.
source: Learning the task took different forms: some mice increased their CR rate, others had a steep increase in hit rate, whereas others gradually increased both hit and CR rates.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Mice learned the task using a range of behavioral strategies.
source: Thus, mice learned the task using a range of behavioral strategies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on behavioral data analysis.

claim: Population responses in the MGB displayed frequency responses, biased to the low frequency range.
source: Population responses in the MGB displayed frequency responses, biased to the low frequency range (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through frequency tuning data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the six mice, the response to the go frequency was significantly higher as compared to the no-go frequency (p<0.05).
source: In the six mice shown below, the response to the go frequency was significantly higher as compared to the no-go frequency (Figure 1G–H, one example mouse; Figure 1I, average of all six mice; p<0.05; Signed rank test; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for the tuning curves of all mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis of frequency tuning data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The tuning curves of individual neurons in the dorsal and medial parts of the MGB are generally broader than ventral MGB.
source: The tuning curves of individual neurons in the dorsal and medial parts of the MGB are generally broader than ventral MGB (Bordi and LeDoux, 1994; Weinberger, 2011), and they represent multiple frequencies (Hackett et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individual neurons in the dorsal and medial parts of the MGB represent multiple frequencies.
source: The tuning curves of individual neurons in the dorsal and medial parts of the MGB are generally broader than ventral MGB (Bordi and LeDoux, 1994; Weinberger, 2011), and they represent multiple frequencies (Hackett et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most recordings were from the dorsal and medial MGB.
source: Whereas we cannot determine the source of the signal explicitly, the fiber tip locations showed that most recordings were from the dorsal and medial MGB.
evidence: This is based on histological reconstruction of fiber tip locations.

claim: The full frequency response areas showed that the signal spanned 2.5 octaves, at least in high intensities.
source: The full frequency response areas showed that our signal spanned 2.5 octaves, at least in high intensities.
evidence: This is based on analysis of frequency response data.

claim: The main source of the fluorescent signal is primarily, though not exclusively, of non-lemniscal origin.
source: Thus, the main source of the fluorescent signal is primarily, though not exclusively, of non-leminsical origin.
evidence: This is inferred from fiber tip locations and frequency response characteristics.

claim: The most evident change in MGB responses across learning was during the late part of the trial (0.6–1 s after stimulus onset), particularly for go trials.
source: The most evident change in MGB responses across learning was during the late part of the trial (0.6–1 s after stimulus onset), and particularly so for go trials (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temporal analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In expert mice, MGB responses were higher for hit as compared to miss trials.
source: In expert mice (defined as the last 500 trials), MGB responses were higher for hit as compared to miss trials, and more so than in the novice mice (defined as the first 500 trials; Figure 2B; compare blue to light blue traces; For comparison, CR and FA trials are plotted in gray; MGB responses for all six mice individually are presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of trial types shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Higher responses in hit versus miss trials were evident in all (6/6) expert mice.
source: Higher responses in hit versus miss trials were evident in all (6/6) expert mice and in 50% (3/6) of novice mice (Figure 2C; p<0.05; Wilcoxon rank sum test for each mouse separately; minimum 40 trials for hit or miss).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Higher responses in hit versus miss trials were evident in 50% (3/6) of novice mice.
source: Higher responses in hit versus miss trials were evident in all (6/6) expert mice and in 50% (3/6) of novice mice (Figure 2C; p<0.05; Wilcoxon rank sum test for each mouse separately; minimum 40 trials for hit or miss).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Choice responses (i.e. hit minus miss) increased gradually after stimulus onset, and were stronger in expert mice.
source: Choice responses (i.e. hit minus miss) increased gradually after stimulus onset, and were stronger in expert mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temporal analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The MGB encodes the choice of the mouse, which implies that the auditory thalamus is involved in higher-level sensory-motor processing or some cognitive attributes of the task.
source: These data suggests that the MGB encodes more than only sounds. MGB encodes the choice of the mouse, which implies that the auditory thalamus is involved in higher-level sensory-motor processing or some cognitive attributes of the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The 'stim-AUC' value is significantly discriminative early in the trial in both the novice and expert cases (<100 ms from stimulus onset).
source: The 'stim-AUC' value is significantly discriminative early in the trial in both the novice and expert cases (Figure 3B,<100 ms from stimulus onset; arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated through AUC analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MGB responses carry highly discriminative information between the stimuli early in the trial and this does not change following learning.
source: This example shows that MGB responses carry highly discriminative information between the stimuli early in the trial and that this does not change following learning.
evidence: This is based on AUC analysis comparing novice and expert conditions.

claim: 'Choice-AUC' reached significance only in the expert condition and only later in the trial (>200 ms from stimulus onset).
source: In contrast, 'choice-AUC' reached significance only in the expert condition and only later in the trial (Figure 3B, green trace,>200 ms from stimulus onset; arrow).
evidence: This is demonstrated through AUC analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The latency of discrimination for 'stim-AUC' was significantly earlier than that of the 'choice-AUC' (p<0.05).
source: The latency of discrimination for 'stim-AUC' was significantly earlier than that of the 'choice-AUC' (Figure 3C; p<0.05; Signed rank test; n = 6 mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The onset of the choice-AUC was significantly earlier than the onset of licking in expert mice (p<0.05).
source: In addition, the onset of the choice-AUC was significantly earlier than the onset of licking in expert mice, implying that choice signal in the MGB precedes the execution of the motor command (p<0.05; Signed Rank test; n = 6 mice; Onset defined in both traces as the peak of the 2nd derivative; Choice onset = 207 ± 109 ms; Lick onset = 385 ± 130 ms; mean ±std).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temporal analysis comparing choice signal and licking onset.

claim: Choice signal in the MGB precedes the execution of the motor command.
source: In addition, the onset of the choice-AUC was significantly earlier than the onset of licking in expert mice, implying that choice signal in the MGB precedes the execution of the motor command (p<0.05; Signed Rank test; n = 6 mice; Onset defined in both traces as the peak of the 2nd derivative; Choice onset = 207 ± 109 ms; Lick onset = 385 ± 130 ms; mean ±std).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between choice-AUC and licking onset.

claim: Stim-AUC was significantly higher than choice-AUC early in the trial (p<0.05).
source: We found that 1) Stim-AUC was significantly higher than choice-AUC early in the trial (p<0.05; Signed rank test; n = 6 mice), 2) Choice-AUC was higher, yet not significantly, during the late part of the trial compared to early times (p=0.09; Signed rank test; n = 6 mice), and 3) Choice-AUC was higher, yet not significantly, in the expert compared to the novice state, particularly during late times during the trial (Figure 3E; p=0.06; Signed rank test; n = 6 mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Stimulus information is present in the MGB relatively early, whereas choice information develops relatively late - several hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset.
source: In summary, these data indicate that stimulus information is present in the MGB relatively early, whereas choice information develops relatively late - several hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on AUC analysis.

claim: The MGB response curve was sigmoid-like, resembling the learning curve of the mouse.
source: The MGB response curve was sigmoid-like, resembling the learning curve of the mouse (Figure 4A shows data from two mice; line is a sigmoid function fit).
evidence: This is demonstrated through curve fitting shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The correlation between MGB response curve and learning curve increased after stimulus onset, indicating a strong relationship between MGB modulations and the learning process.
source: The correlation increased after stimulus onset, indicating a strong relationship between MGB modulations and the learning process (Figure 4B - two representative mice; Figure 4C- all mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated through correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The trial threshold of the MGB curves matched the learning threshold of each mouse (r = 0.89; p<0.05).
source: The trial threshold of the MGB curves matched nicely the learning threshold of each mouse (Figure 4E; r = 0.89; p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated through correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There were no differences between the MGB frequency tuning curves or the response to the go frequency during passive listening, before and after learning.
source: We found no differences between the MGB frequency tuning curves or the response to the go frequency during passive listening, before and after learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that MGB plasticity occurs specifically for task related signals, at least at the population level.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of passive listening responses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MGB plasticity occurs specifically for task related signals, at least at the population level.
source: We found no differences between the MGB frequency tuning curves or the response to the go frequency during passive listening, before and after learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that MGB plasticity occurs specifically for task related signals, at least at the population level.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in passive listening responses.

claim: Changes in MGB responses are positively correlated with learning as evident in similar modulation of the choice signal and the performance of individual mice.
source: In summary, we found that changes in MGB responses are positively correlated with learning as evident in similar modulation of the choice signal and the performance of individual mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on correlation analysis.

claim: Changes in body movements were correlated with learning.
source: As expected, changes in body movements were correlated with learning.
evidence: This is based on analysis of body movement data.

claim: Around the time mice crossed the learning threshold, they exhibited more body movements as evident by plotting their movement probability.
source: Around the time mice crossed the learning threshold, they exhibited more body movements as evident by plotting their movement probability (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated through movement probability analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: During pre-stimulus periods (−1 to 0 relative to stimulus onset) expert mice moved significantly less compared to the novice case (p<0.01).
source: During pre-stimulus periods (−1 to 0 relative to stimulus onset) expert mice moved significantly less compared to the novice case, indicating a higher level of alertness (p<0.01; Signed rank test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis of movement data.

claim: Expert mice moving less during pre-stimulus periods indicates a higher level of alertness.
source: During pre-stimulus periods (−1 to 0 relative to stimulus onset) expert mice moved significantly less compared to the novice case, indicating a higher level of alertness (p<0.01; Signed rank test).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the movement data.

claim: Movement probability during stimulus presentation across learning was sigmoid-like, and significantly higher in experts compared to novice mice (p<0.05).
source: Movement probability during stimulus presentation across learning was sigmoid-like, and significantly higher in experts compared to novice mice (Figure 5C,D; p<0.05; Signed rank test; n = 6 mice).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Body movements during the task are strongly related to the learning process.
source: Thus, as part of the development of choice responses in MGB, the body movements of mice during the task were also strongly related to the learning process.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on movement analysis.

claim: Movement-free MGB responses still encoded the choice of the mouse.
source: Movement-free MGB responses still encoded the choice of the mouse. Specifically, we found higher responses in hit compared to miss trials (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of movement-free signals shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The effect size of choice encoding was smaller and levels of statistical significance were weaker when movement was excluded compared to the signal with movement.
source: Notably, the effect size was smaller and levels of statistical significance were weaker when compared to the signal with movement (Figure 5G; compare to Figure 2C 'Expert').
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of analyses shown in Figure 5G and Figure 2C.

claim: When mice were still novice, movement-free MGB responses did not encode choice, indicating that choice encoding develops with learning, independent of movement.
source: Importantly, when mice were still novice, movement-free MGB responses did not encode choice, indicating that choice encoding develops with learning, independent of movement (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Movement-free MGB responses were enhanced as a function of learning, indicating that enhanced responses in MGB are related to learning processes in ways that are not only directly linked to the movements of the mouse.
source: Indeed, movement-free MGB responses were also enhanced as a function of learning, indicating that enhanced responses in MGB are related to a learning processes in ways that are not only directly linked to the movements of the mouse (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Body movements during the task are evident in the calcium signal and are learning-related.
source: In summary, body movements during the task are evident in the calcium signal and are learning-related.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on movement analysis.

claim: MGB responses maintain choice information that is separate from the motor parameters and develops with learning.
source: Nevertheless, MGB responses still maintains choice information that is separate from the motor parameters and, critically, develops with learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on movement-free signal analysis.

claim: Three additional mice were trained on the task where the go frequency did not correspond to the best frequency.
source: To this end, we trained three additional mice on the task. In these mice, the go frequency did not correspond to the best frequency.
evidence: This describes an additional experimental condition.

claim: In mice tuned away from the go frequency, MGB responses to hit trials were significantly lower than to miss trials in expert mice only (p<0.001).
source: Interestingly, MGB responses in all three mice still showed choice encoding but the absolute direction of change was in the opposite direction as compared to the first cohort of mice (compare Figure 6B to Figure 2C). Specifically, the MGB responses to the hit trials were now significantly lower than to the miss trials and this was evident in expert mice only (Figure 6B; p<0.001; Signed rank test for each mouse separately; minimum 24 trials for hit or miss).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In mice tuned away from the go frequency, choice encoding gradually developed with time along the trial and was evident only in expert mice.
source: In expert mice, choice encoding gradually developed with time along the trial and was evident only in expert mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temporal analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In mice tuned away from the go frequency, MGB response curves were sigmoid-like and strongly correlated with learning.
source: Here again, MGB response curves were sigmoid-like (Figure 6D) and strongly correlated with learning (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through curve fitting and correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Learning enhances responses to the target frequency while simultaneously suppressing activity away from the target frequency.
source: Taken together, we infer that learning enhances responses to the target frequency while simultaneously suppressing activity away from the target frequency.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the two cohorts of mice with different tuning properties.

claim: Both enhancement and suppression phenomena result in the same effect (i.e. encoding of choice), but likely exploit different mechanisms.
source: Notably, both phenomena still result in the same effect (i.e. encoding of choice), but likely exploit different mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Auditory thalamus encodes high-order information during the time course of learning.
source: We describe learning-related changes in evoked responses to sounds in the auditory thalamus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Auditory thalamus encodes the choice of the mouse several hundred milliseconds (~200 ms) after sound onset.
source: We find that auditory thalamus encodes the choice of the mouse several hundred milliseconds (~200 ms; Figure 3C) after sound onset, by specifically enhancing activity to the go frequency as learning proceeds.
evidence: This is demonstrated through temporal analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Auditory thalamus specifically enhances activity to the go frequency as learning proceeds.
source: We find that auditory thalamus encodes the choice of the mouse several hundred milliseconds (~200 ms; Figure 3C) after sound onset, by specifically enhancing activity to the go frequency as learning proceeds.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of learning-related changes.

claim: Late thalamic responses to the same sound are different depending on its learned state.
source: Thus, late thalamic responses to the same sound are different depending on its learned state.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of novice and expert responses.

claim: MGB responses alone allowed prediction with high precision when each mouse learned the task.
source: MGB responses alone allowed us to predict with high precision when each mouse learned the task.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the correlation between MGB response curves and learning thresholds.

claim: Choice encoding in the thalamus bears similarity to observations made in the cortex.
source: Choice encoding in the thalamus (Chen et al., 2019; Gimenez et al., 2015; Jaramillo et al., 2014) bears similarity to the observations made in the cortex (Gilad et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019; Harvey et al., 2012; Pho et al., 2018; Siegel et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016), indicating the intimate involvement of thalamocortical loops during learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in both thalamus and cortex.

claim: The intimate involvement of thalamocortical loops during learning is indicated by similarities in choice encoding between thalamus and cortex.
source: Choice encoding in the thalamus (Chen et al., 2019; Gimenez et al., 2015; Jaramillo et al., 2014) bears similarity to the observations made in the cortex (Gilad et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019; Harvey et al., 2012; Pho et al., 2018; Siegel et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016), indicating the intimate involvement of thalamocortical loops during learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of findings in thalamus and cortex.

claim: The increase in choice signal could arise from small contributions of a large fraction of MGB neurons or from large contributions of a smaller population.
source: The increase in choice signal could arise from small contributions of a large fraction of MGB neurons or from large contributions of a smaller population.
evidence: This is speculation about the cellular basis of the population signal.

claim: A previous study found that only a small fraction (16%) of recorded neurons in MGB encoded choice information.
source: A previous study found that neurons in the MGB (and similarly in cortex) mediate choice but to a limited extent, whereas only a small fraction (16%) of recorded neurons encoded choice information, supporting the latter possibility (Jaramillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Jaramillo et al., 2014 recorded responses from all MGB sub-nuclei, including ventral MGB, while the current measurements were more localized to the medial and dorsal MGB.
source: One noted difference is that Jaramillo et al., 2014 recorded responses from all MGB sub-nuclei, including ventral MGB, while our measurements were more localized to the medial and dorsal MGB.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological differences between studies.

claim: Ventral MGB might not encode choice, and thus previous work may have underestimated the contribution of single neurons in the non-lemniscal pathway in signaling choice.
source: Ventral MGB might not encode choice, and thus previous work may have underestimated the contribution of single neurons in the non-lemniscal pathway in signaling choice.
evidence: This is speculation based on anatomical and functional differences between MGB subdivisions.

claim: Dorsal MGB will likely be affected more prominently by motor parameters compared to the medial MGB.
source: For example, dorsal MGB will likely be affected more prominently by motor parameters compared to the medial MGB (Bartlett et al., 2000; Huang and Winer, 2000; Lee, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Specific populations of MGB neurons that project to different targets will likely transfer specific learning-related information in a selective manner.
source: Further, specific populations of MGB neurons that project to different targets will likely transfer specific learning-related information in a selective manner Chen et al., 2019; as has been shown for the enhancement of choice information in the cortico-striatal pathway (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanisms of plasticity in MGB are unknown and may involve several factors such as inhibitory effects, changes in excitation-inhibition balance, and other forms of synaptic plasticity in specific pathways to the MGB.
source: The mechanisms of this plasticity are unknown and may involve several factors such as inhibitory effects, changes in excitation-inhibition balance, and other forms of synaptic plasticity in specific pathways to the MBG (Audette et al., 2019; McAlonan et al., 2008; Rose and Bonhoeffer, 2018).
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Learning-related dynamics involve disparate circuit elements such as deep cortical layers, specific inhibitory neuron subtypes, or other thalamic sub-nuclei.
source: Learning-related dynamics have been shown to involve disparate circuit elements such as deep cortical layers (Audette et al., 2019; Olsen et al., 2012), specific inhibitory neuron subtypes (Hashikawa et al., 1991; Khan et al., 2018; Peruzzi et al., 1997) or other thalamic sub-nuclei (Audette et al., 2019; Bennett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher-order thalamocortical connections are good candidates to drive synaptic plasticity in cortex during learning.
source: Given that cortex encodes choice, higher-order thalamocortical connections are good candidates to drive synaptic plasticity in cortex during learning (Audette et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The prolonged latency of choice development implies an involvement of a late component that may suggest top-down feedback interaction.
source: The prolonged latency of choice development in our study, implies an involvement of a late component that may suggest top-down feedback interaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the temporal characteristics of choice encoding.

claim: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) could gate incoming sensory information, where in the novice case it is expected to exert strong inhibition to MGB which is then decreased with learning.
source: TRN could gate incoming sensory information, where in the novice case it is expected to exert strong inhibition to MGB which is then decreased with learning; thus enabling enhanced activation to the go sound already at the level of the MGB (McAlonan et al., 2008; Nakajima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Selective disinhibition or inhibition could enhance go-tuned neuronal populations or suppress no-go tuned populations, respectively.
source: Selective disinhibition or inhibition could enhance go-tuned neuronal populations or suppress no-go tuned populations, respectively.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: As mice learn the task, the target frequency enhances activity in tuned population whereas non-tuned populations are simultaneously suppressed.
source: We show that as mice learn the task, the target frequency enhances activity in tuned population whereas non-tuned populations are simultaneously suppressed.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the two cohorts of mice.

claim: This phenomenon may make the target stimulus more salient based on context and bear similarities to other enhancement/suppression mechanisms found in visual thalamus.
source: This phenomenon may make the target stimulus more salient based on context and bear similarities to other enhancement/suppression mechanisms found in visual thalamus (Fisher et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2012; Nakajima et al., 2019; Wilke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to research in visual thalamus.

claim: Medial and dorsal MGB neurons encoding non-target frequencies will be suppressed, whereas the ventral MGB may continue with a similar response profile for all frequencies.
source: Comparing the different MGB subdivisions, we hypothesize that that medial and dorsal MGB neurons encoding non-target frequencies will be suppressed, whereas the ventral MGB may continue with a similar response profile for all frequencies.
evidence: This is speculation about subdivision-specific responses.

claim: Higher-order MGB projects to higher-order auditory cortex (part of the non-lemniscal), and this information may bypass incoming information from the lemniscal pathway and may aid in increasing discrimination performance.
source: Since higher-order MGB projects to higher-order auditory cortex (part of the non-lemniscal), this information may bypass incoming information from the lemniscal pathway and may aid in increasing discrimination performance.
evidence: This is speculation about functional implications of anatomical connectivity.

claim: Motor parameters, such as body movements, are learning-related.
source: We find that motor parameters, such as body movements, are also learning-related.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: As mice learn to associate between the go sound and a reward, they increase their body movement in preparation for licking and the upcoming reward, well within the stimulation period.
source: As mice learn to associate between the go sound and a reward, they increase their body movement in preparation for licking and the upcoming reward, well within the stimulation period.
evidence: This is based on analysis of body movement data.

claim: Movement related encoding may ascend from the inferior colliculus.
source: Another possibility is that movement related encoding may ascend from the inferior colliculus, an upstream area (Gruters and Groh, 2012; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fact that MGB still encodes choice after truncating movement signals indicates that the MGB does not inherit all task information from the inferior colliculus, but rather integrates information coming from both top-down and bottom-up inputs.
source: The fact that MGB still encodes choice after truncating movement signals, indicates that the MGB does not inherit all task information from the inferior colliculus, but rather integrates information coming from both top-down and bottom-up inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of movement-free signals.

claim: The learning process requires brain-wide activity spanning across both cortical and subcortical regions.
source: In summary, we show that the auditory thalamus encodes high-order information during the time course of learning, implying that the learning process requires brain-wide activity spanning across both cortical and subcoritcal regions.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion inferred from the findings.

claim: A total of n = 9, 8–16 week-old female C57BL/6 mice were used in this work.
source: A total of n = 9, 8–16 week-old female C57BL/6 mice were used in this work.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: All experiments were approved by Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel (Permit Number: NS-19-15706-4).
source: All experiments were approved by Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel (Permit Number: NS-19-15706-4).
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval.

claim: 240 nl of AAV virus pAAV.Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 (AAV9) was injected into the dorsal or medial part of the MGB (3.3 mm posterior to bregma; 1.9 mm lateral to bregma; 3 mm in depth).
source: Next, we drilled a small hole in the skull and injected 240 nl of an AAV virus pAAV.Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 (AAV9; from Addgene) using a glass pipette, to the dorsal or medial part of the MGB (3.3 mm posterior to bregma; 1.9 mm lateral to bregma; 3 mm in depth).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: A 400 µm optical fiber with an attached cannula (CFMC14L05; Thorlabs) was inserted directly above the injection site (2.95 mm deep).
source: Using the same coordinates, we then inserted a 400 µm optical fiber with an attached cannula (CFMC14L05; Thorlabs), directly above the injection site (2.95 mm deep).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.
